NoteNlpAccessor::soundex¶

Back to Note NLP Accessor API Reference

Signature¶

Note NoteNlpAccessor::soundex() const

Reduce Each Word To Its Soundex Code¶

soundex() replaces each cell with the Soundex codes of the words it contains, so that names that sound alike collapse to the same key. Robert and Rupert both become R163. Use it for fuzzy name matching, deduplicating a contact list, or building a “sounds-like” index.

The Soundex code¶

Each word is reduced to a letter followed by three digits:

  1. Keep the first letter, upper-cased.

  2. Map the rest to digits — B F P V → 1, C G J K Q S X Z → 2, D T → 3, L → 4, M N → 5, R → 6; vowels and Y produce no digit.

  3. Drop a digit that repeats the one before it (including a first digit that repeats the first letter’s own code).

  4. H and W are transparent: two same-coded consonants separated only by H/W still collapse to one digit (Ashcroft → A261). A vowel or Y between them does not collapse them.

  5. Pad with 0 or truncate so the code is exactly four characters.

This is the NARA / U.S. Census rule set.

Per cell¶

The cell is tokenized into words (letters and digits; punctuation is a separator), each word is coded, and the codes are joined with a single space. "John Smith" → "J500 S530". A cell with no word yields an empty string; a word that is a single letter codes as that letter plus 000.

The operation is shape-preserving and cell-independent, works on UTF-8 text (a bytes-mode Note is rejected with NoteNlpAccessor::soundex requires a UTF-8 text Note (not bytes)), and returns a fresh UTF-8 Note. Non-ASCII letters are not decoded — run to_ascii first if the input has accents.

Example 1: Similar Names Share A Code¶

std::cout << pluss::note::print(
    pluss::make_note({"Robert", "Rupert", "Rubin", "Ashcraft", "Tymczak"})
        .nlp().soundex())
    << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[5], dim=1, numel=5, encoding=utf8)
["R163", "R163", "R150", "A261", "T522"]

Robert and Rupert collapse to R163; Rubin differs at the third digit.

Example 2: H And W Are Transparent¶

std::cout << pluss::note::print(
    pluss::make_note({"Ashcroft", "Pfister"}).nlp().soundex())
    << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[2], dim=1, numel=2, encoding=utf8)
["A261", "P236"]

In Ashcroft the H between s and c (both coded 2) is skipped without breaking the run, so the two 2s become one. In Pfister the leading f repeats P’s own code (1) and is dropped.

Example 3: Multi-Word Cells¶

std::cout << pluss::note::print(
    pluss::make_note({"John Smith", "the quick brown fox"}).nlp().soundex())
    << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[2], dim=1, numel=2, encoding=utf8)
["J500 S530", "T000 Q200 B650 F200"]

Example 4: Short Words And Empty Cells¶

std::cout << pluss::note::print(
    pluss::make_note({"Lee", "A", ""}).nlp().soundex())
    << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[3], dim=1, numel=3, encoding=utf8)
["L000", "A000", ""]

Example 5: Punctuation Is A Separator¶

std::cout << pluss::make_note({"O'Brien, Jr."}).nlp().soundex() << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[1], dim=1, numel=1, encoding=utf8)
["O165 J600"]

O'Brien splits at the apostrophe into O and Brien, coded together as O165; Jr becomes J600.

See Also¶

  • NoteNlpAccessor::metaphone: a consonant-skeleton key that keeps more of the word’s shape than a four-character Soundex code.

  • NoteNlpAccessor::to_ascii: fold accents to ASCII before coding.

  • NoteNlpAccessor::tokens: the word split used per cell.
